doc.title: John Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

chapter: George Shearing and becoming a manager
title: Buddy Rich, then joining the George Shearing Quintet and becoming road manager
summary: Filling in with Buddy Rich at Birdland leads to a permanent bass chair with Shearing; he handles the business and becomes road manager, never playing again.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: when they left to go to California, I decided I was going to quit. So I left that group and this was about the time that I was just sort of like floating around. I got a call to come down to Birdland to work, finish out a week with Buddy Rich. Buddy Rich had a big band. So I went down to Birdland and worked the week with Buddy Rich and George Shearing was playing opposite Buddy Rich. In other words, in those days, in Birdland, there might be three or four different acts. And in this case I think it was George Shearing with Buddy DeFranco and Denzel Best, and who else did he have with him — Margie Hyams I think was the other person that was with him. And this was that group that was playing there. So when my week ended with Buddy Rich, it was only for one week, George Shearing asked me would I join him for a couple of weeks until a bass player that he had that was working with him at the time, could come back. He had to leave because he had some problems and was going to take care of his mother or something, his mother was sick. To make a long story short, he never came back. And I ended up with George Shearing as the bass player in a permanent position. We recorded but the first thing we did we did some things on Discovery label and recorded some tunes and things on that, and then Buddy DeFranco had to leave because he was with MGM and George was with Capitol I think, no it wasn’t Capitol it was MGM, it was the other way around. Buddy DeFranco went with Capitol and George was on MGM. So that’s how we sort of split up. Buddy DeFranco got out of the group and they added Chuck Wayne and that was the beginning of the George Shearing Quintet — the original George Shearing Quintet — which was Denzel Best, Margie Hyams, Chuck Wayne, George Shearing and myself. And then we went on to record for MGM and from that on, “September Rain” and all that stuff, and George became about the hottest attraction in the business. And we were out there and I did all the business for him in other words. Joe Glaser was the agent, and so all the contacts and all the arrangements for everything was done through me. And yet I was just a bass player in there. So finally I said to George, “I can’t do this and play every night.” And we were working a lot of dates on percentage, and I said, “I have to go to the door, and run back and forth, and then come back and play the bass.” So I says, “you’ve got to get somebody else.” So he decided to make me, at that point it was Road Manager was what it was called. And Al McKibbon joined them in my place to play bass. And I became Road Manager. And from that, after maybe six months of that, we got someone else to do the Road Manager because the other business got so heavy, all the deals and everything that you had to be working with, I said I had to stay in New York more and work with the agent. Because George at that time, we’re talking about ‘50 and ‘51, was about the hottest group in the country. We were the number one group. So there was a lot of business to handle. And that’s how I got in to the business end of it. Completely in. From that day on I never played again.
